title: The one who fell short
hook: Arjuna asks the question under every new habit: what if I start, and fail?
carry: no good effort is lost, even across lifetimes

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa and vairagya: Arjuna admitted the mind is restless, Krishna agreed, and gave two oars, practice and letting go. Today, the end of the week, and the end of chapter six.

What about the person who starts with real faith, and can't keep it up? The mind wanders off, and they never get there. Do they lose both worlds? Are they like a small cloud, torn off from the big one, that just thins out and disappears? That's Arjuna's question, the one anyone asks on day nine of a new habit. Six days, six big asks: the same self in every body; the peace that doesn't end; lift the self by the self; a clean place, a firm seat; the lamp out of the wind; the restless mind. That's a lot to live up to.
screen: `WHAT IF I START, AND FAIL?` → `A CLOUD, TORN OFF AND GONE?` → `A WEEK TO LIVE UP TO.`

segments.voice: A painful picture: you left the ordinary life, didn't reach the spiritual one, and now you're neither. Krishna's answer is gentle. Verse forty: there is no destruction for them, Arjuna, neither here nor in the next world. No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end. The word he uses there, tata, is tender, the way an elder speaks to a child. Then he tells what happens. The one who fell short reaches the worlds of the good, and stays long. Then they're born again into a good and prosperous home, or, rarer, into a family of wise yogis. There, verse forty-three says, they get back the understanding they had before, and they strive again, harder. Verse forty-four: they're carried forward by their earlier practice, even without meaning to be. This is the Hindu teaching of karma and rebirth at its gentlest: what you practice leaves a mark on you, and the mark travels with you. Every sit, every returned thought, every day of practice counts, and it carries. So the broken streak doesn't erase the days you kept. Through many lifetimes of effort, the yogi comes to the goal. The chapter ends by lifting the yogi above ascetics, scholars and ritual-doers, and saying that of all yogis, the one who turns to Krishna with faith, the inner self absorbed in him, is the closest. Nothing is lost.
screen: `THE TORN CLOUD.` · `NO ONE WHO DOES GOOD IS LOST.` · `THEY PICK UP WHERE THEY LEFT OFF.` · `EARLIER PRACTICE CARRIES THEM.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Look back over this week, or this whole path so far, to a day you skipped or a sit that was all wandering, and instead of counting it against yourself, picture it the way verse forty-four does: as momentum. Every minute you did sit is still moving you. Breathe in and feel it carrying you; breathe out and let the missed days go.
Tata. My dear: the tender word Krishna uses for Arjuna. Gita six, forty: the one who strives and doesn't arrive isn't lost; earlier practice carries them forward.
Your line: no good effort is lost, even across lifetimes. What you practiced is still moving you. That's chapter six, finished.

howItsDone: Gita 6.40 is often quoted by Hindu teachers to encourage people who have lapsed in practice; some commentators divide the Gita into three sets of six chapters, and chapter six closes the first.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you imagine someone who starts with faith, but their mind wanders and they never arrive. what does Krishna say happens to them?

original.note: Sanskrit: tata, a tender address, 'my dear', used by an elder to a child; Krishna uses it in 6.40.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you quit, it didn't count.
what it means: no one who does good is lost; every bit of practice carries forward, even across lifetimes.

what a scholar hears: 6.38's 'chinnabhram iva', like a torn-off cloud, is answered in 6.40 with 'na hi kalyana-krt kaschid durgatim tata gacchati'; some commentators divide the Gita into three sets of six chapters, and six closes the first.

chat.says: overslept and missed nani's 6am sit this morning 😩 felt like i blew the whole week. nani just said 'nothing is lost, beta' and made me parathas. is that from somewhere??
options: gita 6.40. arjuna asked if someone who starts and falls short ends like a torn cloud. Krishna said no one who does good comes to a bad end; earlier practice carries you on.
she's just being nice. in the gita, missing a day means starting over from nothing.
it means missing doesn't matter, so you never really need to go back.
chat.meaning: The torn cloud was Arjuna's fear. Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to a bad end, and earlier practice carries them on, even into the next life.

tie.story: Arjuna feared that one who starts and falls short ends like a torn cloud, and Krishna said no one who does good is lost; their practice carries them on.

Arjuna.meaning: the warrior prince who questions Krishna in the Gita

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna on the battlefield
